notes:
I could only look at a few sources before my search and page-reading limits ran out. Every note below comes from four commentaries: David Guzik (Enduring Word), the Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott, and a short part of Gill. That means sections 2 and 3 of your brief are mostly empty (see "Not found" at the end).

**Overview**
- Guzik says the theme sits in the last verse: we can defy God and perish, or give in to Him and be blessed. The psalm doesn't name its author, but Acts 4:25–26 says it was David. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-2/
- Ellicott thinks a real political crisis lies behind the psalm. Jerusalem seems threatened by allied enemies who used a young, untested king's coming to the throne as their moment to rebel. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/2.htm People have suggested David, Solomon, Ahaz and Uzziah, but none fits the history exactly. So Ellicott reads the psalm as a picture of an ideal future king. (same URL) He says only that view explains the imperfect fit with history, and that the step from ideal king to Messiah is a small one. (same URL)
- The Pulpit Commentary rates the psalm as clearly Messianic as Isaiah 53. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-2.html

**v. 1**
- Guzik: the psalmist seems truly puzzled. The nations have no reason to rage against God and gain nothing from it, so their opposition is empty. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-2.cfm
- Ellicott's word study: "rage" is better taken as "band together" or "muster." The verb appears only here in this form, and related words point to a plot. The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) has "grown restive," like horses. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/2.htm "Plot" is the same word as "meditate" in Psalm 1:2, used here in a bad sense: muttered treason. (same URL)
- Pulpit: the psalmist sees Jews and Gentiles joined against the gospel. The verse reaches beyond Acts 4 to Christianity's whole struggle, including people today who expect it to fade away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/2.htm
- Gill takes "the peoples" to mean Israel. In his view they plotted in vain when they expected an earthly Messiah and rejected Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/2-1.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik: ever since Babel, people have joined forces against God, wrongly thinking that numbers help. "Anointed" means Christ, so opposing Jesus is opposing the Father. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-2.cfm
- Ellicott: "Messiah" first meant anyone anointed for a holy office. Its special sense of a promised deliverer-prince may go back mainly to this psalm. The New Testament quotes the psalm often, which shows how Jewish tradition understood it. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/2.htm
- Pulpit: in David's day "the Lord's anointed" was Israel's king, first Saul and then David. Here David seems to point past himself to the true King he foreshadowed. Historical examples of hostile "kings" and "rulers" include the Herods, Nero, Diocletian and the Sanhedrin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/2.htm

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: wicked people always feel God's rule and law as restraints. "Chains" and "cords" are prisoners' fetters that the rebels want to burst. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/2.htm
- Guzik: the rebels see God as someone who enslaves. That is spiritual madness, because God breaks bondage. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-2.cfm He quotes Spurgeon: Christ's yoke feels unbearable to the unsaved but light to the saved. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-2/
- Ellicott: the whispered plan now becomes a loud threat. The Septuagint and Latin Vulgate read "yoke." https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/2.htm

**v. 4**
- Pulpit: God's laughter and scorn are human pictures for God. They mean He treats rebellion with contempt. People will obey God, willingly or unwillingly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/2.htm
- Guzik: God is seated, calm and not pacing. Quoting G. Campbell Morgan, he says God doesn't enjoy sinners' suffering but mocks their proud attempts to block His will. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-2.cfm
- Ellicott: where we talk of the "irony of events," the Hebrew credits that irony to God, who controls events. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/2.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: God speaks before He acts. That warning shows His mercy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-2.cfm
- Pulpit: God "speaks" through what actually happens, not through an audible voice. The Church outlived every persecution. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/2.htm
- Ellicott: "terrifies" is an intensive verb, literally "in His nostrils and in His heat." https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/2.htm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: "I" is emphatic: "it is I who gave the king this office." "Installed" literally means "poured," as with molten metal. Some scholars render it "anointed." The Septuagint and Vulgate make the King start speaking here. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/2.htm
- Pulpit: God is speaking. It allows some reference to David but sees Christ as the main subject, King forever in the heavenly Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/2.htm
- Guzik: God wants the rebel kings to know there is a greater King, set in place in Zion. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-2.cfm

**v. 7** (the main point of difference among these sources)
- Guzik: the Anointed One is speaking. Hebrews 1:5 uses the verse to prove Jesus is divine and greater than angels. "Begotten" is the opposite of "created": a man makes a statue but fathers a child. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-2.cfm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-2/
- Pulpit: the decree was made by the Father "in the beginning of all things." "My Son" means the one and only Son. But it says "today" is the day Christ began His saving work, when the Father handed Him rule over creation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/2.htm
- Ellicott: the king recalls what God promised him at his coronation. "Today" is that coronation day, a kind of new birthday for the king or the monarchy. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/2.htm He links this to 2 Samuel 7:14 and Psalm 89, and says the whole line of tradition reads it as Messianic. (same URL)
- So these sources give three answers for what "today" means: Guzik stresses the Son's divine nature, Pulpit the start of His saving work, and Ellicott the original coronation. I did not find any denomination's own teachers addressing this.

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: David ruled only a small part of the nations, so this can only be about the Messiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/2.htm
- Guzik: all judgment belongs to Christ (John 5:22). He links the verse to Revelation 11:15. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-2/
- Pulpit's sermon notes: the inheritance is moral, not material. It comes by right, not force, and the nations must be won by truth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-2.html

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: the Septuagint has "you will shepherd them," taking the rod as a shepherd's staff. Ellicott thinks shattering pottery points to a rod of punishment. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/2.htm
- Pulpit: some scholars say this "cannot describe the mild rule of Christ." Pulpit disagrees, pointing to Romans 11:22, Matthew 10:34 and Revelation 2:27 and 19:15. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/2.htm
- Pulpit's sermon notes: those who refuse Christ's sceptre of grace will feel His iron rod. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-2.html

**v. 10**
- Pulpit: this is the psalmist's advice to the rebels and anyone who copies them: give up, because God and Messiah can't be resisted. Compare Gamaliel in Acts 5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/2.htm
- Ellicott: the Latin of this verse was the motto on an English medal struck after Charles I was executed. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/2.htm
- Guzik: if kings must bow, so must everyone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-2/

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: serve from fear if not from love, then move on from fear to love and joy. Rejoicing still needs reverence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/2.htm
- Ellicott: "trembling" literally means quaking, which can come from joy or from fear. Old translations paraphrase it as "pray," "cleave to him" or "praise him." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-2.html

**v. 12** (disputed translation)
- Guzik keeps "Kiss the Son": it is mainly a kiss of submission, with a hint of affection. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-2.cfm
- Pulpit also keeps it. It admits the word for "son" here (*bar*) differs from v. 7 (*ben*), but finds *bar* in Proverbs 31:2 and calls it an old, poetic word for high rank. It reads the kiss as royal homage (1 Samuel 10:1). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/2.htm
- Ellicott disagrees. He says "this familiar translation must be surrendered," because all the ancient versions except the Syriac are against it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-2.html He argues the psalmist would hardly switch from *ben*, and that most rabbis are also against it. His suggested reading is "proffer pure homage" to God. (same URL)
- "In an instant" is better read as "his wrath is soon kindled" (Ellicott, Pulpit). (Ellicott, same URL)
- The closing blessing softens the psalm's severity (Pulpit). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/2.htm
- Guzik sums up the final choice as "broken or blessed?" https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-2.cfm

**Not found (left out)**
- I found no teachers writing as Baptist, Methodist, Lutheran, Reformed or Pentecostal on Psalm 2.
- I read nothing from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. The closest thing to a modern-scholarship view is Ellicott's notes on the historical setting and v. 12.
- I found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace material on this psalm.
- Next places to check: the netbible.org notes on vv. 7 and 12, Augustine's sermon on Psalm 2 at newadvent.org, gotquestions.org on "Kiss the Son," and desiringgod.org or gty.org on "today I have begotten you."
